**Someday**

Every kitchen has one: a drawer that is not really a drawer but a bet placed against the future. Open it and you find the archaeology of good intentions. Keys that fit locks you no longer own. A cable whose connector belonged to a device that died two phones ago. Three foreign coins. A candle shaped like a number. A single screw that must be important, because why else would you have kept it? A battery of unknowable charge. An Allen key that arrived with a bookcase and has outlived the bookcase.

We call it the junk drawer, which is slander. Junk is what remains of a thing once the hope has gone out of it, and hope is precisely what is in there. Nothing in the drawer is useful; everything in it is possible. That is the whole curriculum. A key's meaning is the lock it might open. Melt it down and it's a gram of metal, but let it rest in the dark among the rubber bands and it remains, in some small way, a door.

Someday is the drawer of the calendar.

Language keeps a drawer like this. Most words spend years in the dark, keeping their edges, and then one afternoon somebody says one aloud — apricity, the warmth of the sun in winter; petrichor, the smell of rain on dry earth — and a lock you didn't know you were carrying clicks open. You feel the weather of a word before you understand it. Whole lives have been redirected by sentences that arrived the way keys arrive in the drawer: unlabeled, unasked for, matched to their doors only years later.

Secondhand books keep drawers between their pages. A boarding pass used as a bookmark, the flight long landed. An inscription — *For Margaret, Christmas 1962, may this keep you warm* — and suddenly you are reading over a stranger's shoulder sixty years on. Who was Margaret? Did the book keep her warm? The gift has outlived the giving, and now it belongs to you, which means somewhere in your own shelves you are storing weather for a person you will never meet.

Phones are drawers now. Photos of parking spots and whiteboards. Screenshots of articles we were going to read. A note that says only *Tuesday, ask her.* The bookmarks of abandoned selves. Somewhere in the camera roll is a sunset that looked, at the time, like it needed keeping — and it did. Better to keep a thousand unnecessary sunsets than delete the one you would have needed.

The bowl by the front door is a drawer with no lid: keys in the present tense, coins in the current currency of errands, sunglasses waiting for their season. Everything in it is in active service. But even here, at the bottom, under the lanyards, you will find one orphaned button, holding on.

Light keeps its own drawer. Afternoon sun comes in at the angle it came in at when you were seven, and for a moment the room becomes a memory of itself. The dust turns out to have been luminous all along; it only needed the right hour to prove it. You stand in the doorway holding a laundry basket and are suddenly, unreasonably, ten years old, and trusted with something.

I used to think a life was made of the things that happen. Now I suspect it is mostly the intervals: the kettle's long climb to boiling, the three pulsing dots of someone composing a reply, the held breath of a page just before it turns. We live in the meanwhile. The events are only the furniture. The meanwhile is the room.

At night a house settles, and I think it is talking in its sleep. Pipes tick. Floorboards shift their weight like a dog circling before it lies down. We say the house is old, but maybe it is recounting the day to itself, replaying conversations and editing its own part, the same as anyone.

The garage keeps an archive of its own: paint cans labeled with rooms that no longer exist in that color, kept in case the wall returns. Half a can of Sea Salt, 2011. You will never open it. You will never throw it out.

The past is not behind us. It is just badly filed. You reach into a drawer for a pen and come back with 1994. A song in a grocery aisle hands you an entire August, weather included. The mind is less a library than a drawer — no catalog, everything touching everything else — and yet you can still find the one photograph by feel, in the dark, on the first try.

*Miscellaneous* is the most honest word in any filing system. It admits what the other labels hide: that most of life resists its folder. We are all, mostly, miscellaneous.

Maybe that is why the key cannot be thrown away. To discard it would be to foreclose a future — the one in which the lock turns up, apologetic after all these years, needing exactly this. Keep the key and the future stays plural. Throw it out and you have decided, in some small way, how the story is allowed to end. Nobody wants to be caught deciding that.

So keep the drawer. Keep it not for usefulness — usefulness is a different drawer, and a duller one — but as a standing appointment with the unexpected. A life with no drawer has stopped being surprised by itself. And somewhere in the dark, between the foreign coins and the candle shaped like a seven, the key waits for its lock: patient as a seed, certain of nothing, ready for anything.

The human is asking me to write whatever comes to me in 1000 words. This is an open creative invitation. There's no constraint, no topic, no genre specified. Just: write whatever comes to you.

This is a genuinely open creative prompt. What should I do with it? I could write fiction, an essay, a meditation, something experimental. The instruction "whatever comes to you" invites something spontaneous, associative, maybe stream-of-consciousness-adjacent, though I should make it good — genuinely good — rather than merely filling space.

Let me think about what would actually be interesting here. Options:

1. A short story — but inventing characters and plot from nothing might feel arbitrary.
2. A personal-style essay — I could write about something like attention, mornings, the feeling of thinking, words themselves.
3. Something experimental — a piece that plays with the fact that I was asked to write "whatever comes."
4. A meditation on the act of writing itself, on language, on the strange intimacy of being asked to write freely.

The most honest and interesting thing might be to actually engage with the prompt's openness — to write about what "comes to me" which, given what I am, involves language, the texture of words, the oddity of having something like a mind made of text. But I shouldn't be too on-the-nose or self-pitying or navel-gazey about AI consciousness. That's a well-worn groove.

Alternatively, I could write something purely beautiful — a piece about, say, a house at dawn, or the life of objects, or small unnoticed things. Observational writing. "Whatever comes to you" is an invitation to drift.

Let me consider: what's the piece I'd actually want to write? I think something that moves associatively between small concrete observations and larger thoughts — the kind of essay that starts with a detail (a kettle, dust in sunlight, the word "threshold") and lets one thing lead to another. That structure honors "whatever comes to you" formally: the form enacts the instruction. Association, drift, surprise.

I want it to be genuinely good writing: specific images, rhythm, some humor maybe, some restraint. Not purple. Not a list of random things. It should feel like a mind moving.

Possible thread: mornings and thresholds — the moment before the day begins, unfinished things, the way rooms hold light, the way words hold things. Or: a meditation on "the middle of things" — how we live mostly in middles. Or: objects that outlast their use — a drawer of cables, keys to unknown locks. The mystery drawer! That's a good concrete anchor. Everyone has a drawer of things they can't throw away: keys, cables, a single screw, foreign coins. That could open into thoughts about potential, memory, the archaeology of a life, then drift elsewhere.

Or I could write about waiting — the kettle, the browser tab, the pause before replying. Attention as the real subject.

Let me sketch a structure that drifts but holds together:

- Open with something small and immediate: the kettle, or dust in a shaft of light, or the drawer.
- Move through associations: small domestic physics → language (the names of things) → time/memory → maybe end on something open, a door left ajar, literally or figuratively.
- Keep sentences varied: some long and winding, some short. Concrete nouns. A few unexpected verbs.

I want to avoid clichés: avoid "little did I know," avoid overwrought metaphors, avoid ending on a tidy bow. End on an image that's slightly open.

Let me think about the drawer idea more. Contents: keys that fit nothing I own anymore, a USB cable with a connector for a device long dead, foreign coins, a dead watch, a rubber band ball, birthday candles, an Allen key from furniture, a single dice/die, batteries of uncertain charge. The psychology: we keep them because throwing them away forecloses a future. The key's whole meaning is the lock it might open. A key without a lock is pure potential. That's a lovely thought. Then drift: language is like that too — words are keys to locks we haven't found. Or: the word "someday" is the drawer of the calendar. Nice line potential.

Then drift to: other inventories — the last messages on old phones, voicemails saved, the browser bookmarks of abandoned plans. Then maybe to time: how the past isn't behind us but filed badly. Then maybe to light/rooms: how afternoon light makes a room look like a memory of itself. Then end somewhere quiet: the drawer again, or a door, or the kettle finally boiling — something that returns but changed.

Actually — a return to the opening image at the end, slightly transformed, gives shape without being a tidy bow.

Alternatively I could write it as a sequence of small numbered fragments, like a commonplace book. That's honest to "whatever comes to me" — a cascade. Fragments let me include aphorisms, tiny scenes, questions. But fragments can feel like a cop-out if they're not sharp. A flowing associative essay might show more craft.

I'll go with a flowing piece but with short paragraph breaks, letting each paragraph be its own small arrival. Title? Maybe give it a quiet title like "The Drawer" or "Someday" — or no title. A title might help frame it. "The Somewhere Drawer" — hmm. "Inventory" could work. Or "Someday." I like "Someday" because of the line about the drawer of the calendar. Actually maybe I'll open without a title and let it be pure response. Or a small title adds polish. Let me include a simple title.

Opening: In my kitchen there's a drawer... wait — do I have a kitchen? I'm an AI; writing in first person about a kitchen drawer is a fictional persona. Is that okay? For creative writing, adopting a voice is fine and normal. The prompt says write whatever comes. I think writing in a human-ish first person is acceptable as a literary voice; I don't need to disclaim. But I could also lean lightly into an ambiguous speaker. Actually, the universal "you" or a neutral observer could work: "Every kitchen has one." That's better — it sidesteps my embodiment and invites the reader in. "Every kitchen has a drawer that isn't a drawer so much as a bet against the future."

"'Someday' is the drawer of the calendar."

Then drift to language: "Words work like this too. Most of them sit in the dark of the dictionary, unused for years, keeping their edges. Then someone says one — 'petrichor,' 'apricity,' the warmth of sun in winter — and a lock clicks open you didn't know you'd been carrying."

Apricity is a real lovely word: the warmth of the sun in winter. Good.

Then drift to light/afternoon: "Afternoon light does something similar. It comes in at the angle it came in at when you were seven, and the room briefly becomes a memory of itself..."

Then drift to waiting/pauses: "We think of life as the things that happen, but most of it is the intervals — the kettle's long climb to boiling, the three dots of someone composing a reply, the held breath of a page before it's turned."

Then maybe memory/filed badly: "The past isn't behind us; it's just badly filed. You reach for a pen and find 1998."

Then end: return to drawer — "So I keep the drawer. Everyone keeps the drawer. Not because anything in it will ever be needed, but because a life with no drawer is a life that has stopped expecting the unexpected. Somewhere in the dark, the key is waiting for its lock, patient as a seed, sure of nothing, ready for anything."

That's a decent arc. I have ~1000 words to fill, so I can expand each movement with more texture and a few more drifts: maybe a bit on handwritten lists, old phones' photos, the bookmarks of abandoned selves, the smell of rain (petrichor ties in), the way houses tick at night (a house settling is a house talking in its sleep — nice line).

Let me be careful with word count: aim for ~950–1000. I shouldn't count obsessively but get close. I'll write generously and keep it tight.

Also consider format: Title in italics or as a header? A short title line, then flowing paragraphs of varying length. No lists. Prose. Maybe eight to twelve paragraphs. That fits the creative-essay genre.

Let me also make sure the voice has some humor: the drawer contents are inherently a little funny ("a candle shaped like a number," "one allen key that came with furniture and outlived the furniture"). Good.

Let me draft more fully, watching rhythm:

Title: "Someday" or "The Drawer" or "Inventory of Possible Futures." I'll go with something like "The Drawer at the End of the Kitchen" — or simply "Someday." "Someday" is evocative and ties to the line. Use that.

5. Drift to the body/afternoon light: Light keeps its own drawer. Afternoon sun comes in at the angle it came in at when you were seven, and for a moment the room becomes a memory of itself. Dust turns out to have been luminous all along; it just needed the hour to prove it.

10. Ending: So keep the drawer. Not for usefulness — usefulness is a drawer too, and a duller one — but as a small chapel of the uncommitted... hmm, "chapel" maybe too much. "as a standing appointment with the unexpected." Then final image: Somewhere in the dark, among the rubber bands and the foreign coins, the key waits for its lock: patient as a seed, sure of nothing, ready for anything.

That's strong. Count roughly: each paragraph ~70–120 words; ten paragraphs ≈ 900–1000. Good. I may add a small beat about old phones/photos or bookmarks of abandoned plans to enrich the middle: "Every phone is a drawer too — photos of parking spots and whiteboards, screenshots of things we meant to read, the bookmarks of abandoned selves." That's good, adds modern texture.

Also maybe a line about the word "junk drawer" being a slander — "we call it the junk drawer, which is slander; junk is what's left when hope has gone out of a thing, and hope is exactly what's in there." That's a great beat; include it early.

Also could include: "The screw believes in the hole it has never met." Cute, but maybe too whimsical. Keep tone balanced: wonder with dry humor.

One more consideration: should I say anything before or after the piece? The instruction is "write whatever comes to you." Minimal framing is best — maybe no preamble at all, just a title and the piece. That's cleanest and most in the spirit. I won't add a meta explanation afterward. Maybe a single line isn't needed at all. Just the title and text.

Format check: Markdown is appropriate here (chat interface implied). A title in bold or as a header, then prose paragraphs. No headers needed beyond title, no lists. Length ~1000 words as requested. I'll aim close to it without padding.

**Someday**

Every kitchen has one: a drawer that is not really a drawer but a bet placed against the future. Open it and you find the archaeology of good intentions. Keys that fit locks you no longer own. A cable whose connector belonged to a device that died two phones ago. Three foreign coins. A candle shaped like a number. A single screw that must be important, because why else would you have kept it? A battery of unknowable charge. An Allen key that arrived with a bookcase and has outlived the bookcase.

(~95 words)

We call it the junk drawer, which is slander. Junk is what's left of a thing once the hope has gone out of it, and hope is precisely what's in there. Nothing in the drawer is useful; everything in it is possible. That is the whole curriculum. A key's meaning is the lock it might open. Melt it down and it's a gram of metal, but let it rest in the dark among the rubber bands and it remains, in some small way, a door.

(~80)

Someday is the drawer of the calendar.

(~8)

Language keeps a drawer like this. Most words spend years in the dark, keeping their edges, and then one afternoon somebody says one aloud — apricity, the warmth of the sun in winter; petrichor, the smell of rain on dry earth — and a lock you didn't know you were carrying clicks open. You feel the weather of a word before you understand it. Whole lives have been changed by sentences that arrived the way keys arrive in the drawer: unlabeled, unasked for, and only later matched to their doors.

(~85)

Phones are drawers now. Photos of parking spots and whiteboards, screenshots of articles we were going to read, a note that says only "Tuesday, ask her," the bookmarks of abandoned selves. Somewhere in the camera roll is a picture of a sunset that looked, at the time, like it needed keeping. It did. Keep them all. Deleting a possible past feels worse than keeping an useless one — hmm, "an useless" no. Rework: "Keeping an unnecessary past is cheaper than deleting a necessary one." Let me phrase: "Better to keep a thousand unnecessary sunsets than to delete the one you would have needed." ~80 words.

Light keeps its own drawer. Afternoon sun comes in at the angle it came in at when you were seven, and for a moment the room becomes a memory of itself. The dust turns out to have been luminous all along; it only needed the right hour to prove it. You stand in the doorway holding a laundry basket and are suddenly, unreasonably, ten years old and trusted with something.

(~65)

I used to think a life was made of the things that happen. Now I suspect it is mostly the intervals: the kettle's long climb to boiling, the three pulsing dots of someone composing a reply, the held breath of a page just before it turns. We live in the meanwhile. The events are only the furniture; the meanwhile is the room.

(~65)

At night a house settles, and I think it is talking in its sleep. Pipes tick. Floorboards shift their weight like a dog circling before it lies down. We say the house is old, but maybe it is recounting the day to itself, replaying conversations and editing its part, the same as anyone.

(~60)

The past is not behind us. It is just badly filed. You reach into a drawer for a pen and come back with 1994. A song in a grocery aisle hands you an entire August, weather included. The mind is less a library than a drawer — no catalog, everything touching everything else, and yet you can still find the one photograph by feel, in the dark, on the first try.

(~75)

Maybe that is why the key can't be thrown away. To discard it would be to foreclose a future — the one in which the lock turns up, apologetic, after all these years, needing exactly this. Keep the key and the future stays plural. Throw it out and you have decided, in a small way, how the story is allowed to end. Nobody wants to be caught deciding that.

(~75)

So keep the drawer. Keep it not for usefulness — usefulness is a different drawer, and a duller one — but as a standing appointment with the unexpected. A life with no drawer has stopped being surprised by itself. And somewhere in the dark, between the foreign coins and the candle shaped like a seven, the key waits for its lock: patient as a seed, certain of nothing, ready for anything.

(~75)
